'''Mary Jo Ondrechen''' (born 1953) is an American chemist, educator, researcher, community leader and activist. She is a professor of chemistry and chemical biology and principal investigator <ref name="one">[http://www.northeastern.edu/cos/faculty/mary-jo-ondrechen/ Northeastern University College of Science Faculty - Chemistry and Chemical Biology]. (2014).</ref> of the [[computational biology]] research group at [[Northeastern University]] in [[Boston, Massachusetts]].

== Education ==

Ondrechen received an [[American Chemical Society]] certified bachelor's degree in chemistry from [[Reed College]], [[Portland, Oregon]], in 1974. She pursued doctoral studies in chemistry and chemical physics at [[Northwestern University]], [[Evanston, Illinois]], and earned the Ph.D. degree in 1978 under the direction of [[Mark A. Ratner]].<ref name="two">{{cite web|url=http://chemgroups.northwestern.edu/ratner/|title=Ratner Group – Home of the Ratner Research Group|website=chemgroups.northwestern.edu}}</ref> After postdoctoral research appointments at the [[University of Chicago]] and at [[Tel-Aviv University]] in [[Israel]], the latter as a [[NATO]] postdoctoral fellow, she joined the faculty at Northeastern University in Boston, Massachusetts in 1980.<ref name="three">Pollastri, M.P. [http://www.northeastern.edu/cos/chemistry/faculty-4/] (2017)</ref>

== Research and discoveries ==

Her earlier research achievements include the design of [[molecules]] and materials with desirable spectroscopic and conductive properties, prediction of electric field effects in molecules and [[proteins]], the optimization of energy conversion devices, and the design and characterization of ionic conductor materials for rechargeable [[Battery (electricity)|batteries]]. Her current research activities include modeling of biological [[macromolecules]]<ref name="four">Finley, A., [http://www.sdsc.edu/pub/envision/v15.4/ondrechen.html Investigating Enzyme-Substrate Interactions with Vitamin B6]. (1999).</ref> and predictive calculations for [[functional genomics]].

She co-developed [[THEMATICS]]<ref name="five">[https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2001/10/011030225809.htm Protein Function Predicted With New "THEMATICS" Method Developed By Northeastern University & Brandeis Scientists]. ScienceDaily, (2001).</ref><ref name="six">Borman, S., From sequence to consequence. Chemical and Engineering News,  79(48): p. 31-33 (2001).</ref><ref name="seven">Ball, P., [http://www.nature.com/news/2001/011019/full/news011025-1.html Computers spot shape clues]. Nature, (2001).</ref> (Theoretical Microscopic Anomalous Titration Curve Shapes), a computational predictor of functional information about proteins from their three-dimensional structure alone. THEMATICS predicts catalytic and [[binding sites]] in proteins with high sensitivity and good selectivity. A unique feature of THEMATICS is that it requires neither sequence nor structural comparisons and hence applies to novel folds, orphan sequences, and also to engineered [[polypeptide]] systems.

She is also the co-developer, with Wenxu Tong and [[Ronald J. Williams]], of a [[machine learning]] technology called Partial Order Optimum Likelihood (POOL).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tong|first1=Wenxu|last2=Wei|first2=Ying|last3=Murga|first3=Leonel F.|last4=Ondrechen|first4=Mary Jo|last5=Williams|first5=Ronald J.|date=2009-01-16|title=Partial Order Optimum Likelihood (POOL): Maximum Likelihood Prediction of Protein Active Site Residues Using 3D Structure and Sequence Properties|url= |journal=PLOS Computational Biology|volume=5|issue=1|article-number=e1000266|doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000266|pmid=19148270|pmc=2612599|bibcode=2009PLSCB...5E0266T|issn=1553-7358 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Somarowthu|first1=Srinivas|last2=Yang|first2=Huyuan|last3=Hildebrand|first3=David G. C.|last4=Ondrechen|first4=Mary Jo|date=2011-06-01|title=High-performance prediction of functional residues in proteins with machine learning and computed input features|journal=Biopolymers|volume=95|issue=6|pages=390–400|doi=10.1002/bip.21589|issn=0006-3525|pmid=21254002}}</ref> POOL is a monotonicity-constrained maximum likelihood method for the prediction of properties that depend monotonically on the input features. This method, coupled with THEMATICS input features, is a top-performing [[active site]] predictor for protein structures.{{cn|date=March 2025}}

These methods are also being used for the successful annotation of [[structural genomics]] proteins, i.e. for the discovery of the function of gene products whose function is currently unknown. Her Structurally Aligned Local Sites of Activity (SALSA) method uses local sets of [[amino acid]] residues that are computationally predicted to be active in catalysis to identify the biochemical function of [[enzyme]] structures of unknown function.

These computational methods are also currently used to understand how enzymes affect [[catalysis]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ondrechen|first1=Mary Jo|last2=Clifton|first2=James G.|last3=Ringe|first3=Dagmar|date=2001-10-23|title=THEMATICS: A simple computational predictor of enzyme function from structure|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=98|issue=22|pages=12473–12478|doi=10.1073/pnas.211436698|issn=0027-8424|pmc=60078|pmid=11606719|bibcode=2001PNAS...9812473O|doi-access=free}}</ref> Ondrechen has emphasized and developed the concept of spatially extended enzyme active sites, and that the participation of [[amino acids]], even if they are distant from the site of the catalyzed reaction, may be predicted with a relatively simple calculation.<ref name="eight">Herring, A., [http://phys.org/news/2012-04-function-enzyme.html Form and function in enzyme activity]. (2012).</ref>

Her research group has also developed computational methods to improve the design of artificial enzymes.{{cn|date=March 2025}}

In 2020 Ondrechen's research group added a new project to characterize the proteins of [[SARS-CoV-2]], the virus that causes [[COVID-19]], and to seek interventions to disrupt the viral life cycle <ref name="nine">https://www.metrowestdailynews.com/news/20200501/hopkinton-resident-receives-national-science-foundation-grant-to-study-coronavirus Hopkinton resident receives National Science Foundation grant to study coronavirus.</ref><ref name="ten">https://news.northeastern.edu/2020/05/15/the-coronavirus-might-have-hidden-weak-spots-machine-learning-could-help-find-them/ The coronavirus might have hidden weak spots. Machine learning could help find them.</ref>

She was the 2024 recipient of the Technical Excellence Award of AISES <ref>https://aises.org/aises-announces-2024-professional-award-winners</ref> and the 2026 Lifetime Mentoring Award of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) <ref name="fifteen">https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-announces-2026-award-winners</ref>

== Community activism ==

Ondrechen is a community leader and activist. She has recently served on the board of advisors of the [[Washington, D.C.]]–based [[Interstate Technology and Regulatory Council]] (ITRC), representing the interests of community and tribal stakeholders.<ref name="sixteen">Willett, A., [http://www.itrcweb.org/Documents/2012_ITRC_Board_of_Advisors1.pdf] (2012)</ref> She is the former president of the board of directors of the North American Indian Center of Boston ([[NAICOB]])<ref name="seventeen">Dunn, J., [http://www.naicob.org/about-us.html About NAICOB]. (2013).</ref> and served as chair of the board of directors of the Albuquerque, New Mexico-based American Indian Science and Engineering Society ([[AISES]]) from 2011 to 2013.<ref name="eighteen">EchoHawk, S., [http://www.aises.org/about/board AISES Board of Directors]. (2014).</ref> An advocate for stewardship of the Earth, she previously has served on the Conservation Commission for [[Hopkinton, Massachusetts]], and on the Community Leaders Network of the [[U.S. Department of Energy]]. She has been active in the promotion of innovative technologies to solve environmental problems.<ref name="nineteen">[http://redox-tech.com/doc_download/47-itrc-chemox.html In Situ Chemical Oxidation]. (2000).</ref><ref name="twenty">[http://www.orau.org/ptp/PTP%20Library/library/Subject/Decommissioning/TRIAD-T1.pdf Technical and Regulatory Guidance for the Triad Approach: A New Paradigm for Environmental Project Management]. (2003).</ref><ref name="twenty-one">[https://www.scribd.com/doc/46813094/Dpt-Wells-for-Gwm-Itrc The Use of Direct Push Well Technology for Long-term Environmental Monitoring in Groundwater Investigations]. (2006).</ref> She also advocates for the inclusion of public and tribal stakeholders in environmental evaluation, decision-making, and management.

She was a speaker at the [[March for Science]] in Washington, D.C. in April 2017.<ref name="twenty-two">{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/speaking-of-science/wp/2017/04/20/why-scientists-are-marching-on-washington-and-more-than-400-other-cities/ |title=Why scientists are marching on Washington and more than 600 other cities |date=2017-04-21 |author1=Joel Achenbach |author2=Ben Guarino |author3=Sarah Kaplan |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |place=Washington, D.C. |issn=0190-8286 |oclc=1330888409}}</ref><ref name="twenty-three">{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mucx9adauQQ|title = Prof. Mary Jo Ondrechen at the March for Science|website = [[YouTube]]| date=23 April 2017 }}</ref>

She has given numerous presentations on diversity and inclusiveness in the science, technology, engineering, and mathematics ([[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]]) fields.<ref>Hernandez, R., [http://www.oxide.gatech.edu/ver1.0/index.html?ondrechen.html&2&bios&3 OXIDE Biography: Mary Jo Ondrechen]. (2014).</ref><ref>[http://www.pathwaystoscience.org/profiles.aspx?ind=OndreMaryJ Pathways to Science, Mary Jo Ondrechen]. (2012).</ref>
